title: Symmetry-Tunable Skyrmions and Merons in Magnetic Nanodisks via Spatially Engineered Anisotropy
authors: X. D. Wang, J. F. Oliveira da Silva, Z. H. Tao, H. M. Dong, K. Chang, M. V. Milošević
abstract: We demonstrate that spatially engineered magnetic anisotropy can stabilize skyrmion and meron spin textures in magnetic nanodisks even in the absence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). Using a constrained analytical model and micromagnetic simulations, we show that competing perpendicular and in-plane anisotropies can generate non-collinear topological textures in non-chiral magnetic systems. We further show that DMI and dipolar interactions lift the helicity degeneracy and select preferred chiral configurations; micromagnetic simulations were used to identify physically stable states. These results establish anisotropy-patterned nanodisks as a platform for studying DMI-free topological spin textures and their controllable magnetic response. We also show that arrays of anisotropy-engineered skyrmions can control spin-wave transmission by manipulating their vorticity arrangement, pointing to reconfigurable magnonic elements based on non-chiral topological textures.
summary: This work demonstrates that magnetic skyrmion and meron textures can be stabilized in nanodisks purely by patterning the magnetocrystalline anisotropy, bypassing the need for the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Using micromagnetic simulations, the authors show this patterned structure allows for deterministic control over topology and, crucially, enables arrays of these defects to act as reconfigurable elements for controlling spin-wave transmission.
main_problem: The primary goal is stabilizing tunable skyrmion and meron spin textures in magnetic nanodisks without relying on the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). This addresses limitations in using centrosymmetric magnets.
main_result: Spatially engineered anisotropy, combining perpendicular and in-plane components, can deterministically stabilize these topological textures. Furthermore, arrays of such structures can be used to control spin-wave transmission by manipulating vorticity arrangement.
method: The study employs a combination of constrained analytical modeling and unconstrained micromagnetic simulations to solve the governing partial differential equation derived from minimizing the total energy functional.
model_or_system: The system is magnetic nanodisks where the magnetization dynamics are governed by an energy functional incorporating exchange, anisotropy (both perpendicular and in-plane), dipolar, and DMI terms. The key mechanism involves patterning the anisotropy to break symmetry artificially.
key_observables: Topological charge (Q), in-plane spin configurations, and transverse deflection/control of transmitted spin waves (SW).
important_parameters: The relative strengths of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy ($K_{	ext{PMA}}$) versus engineered in-plane uniaxial anisotropy ($	ext{IMA}$); the presence or absence of DMI.
main_assumptions: The model utilizes the Landau-Lifshitz continuum approximation, and while presented as generalizable, specific material choices are suggested for validation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic models showing skyrmion/meron stabilization via anisotropy patterning (IMA ring in PMA background), show spin configurations with and without DMI, and demonstrate SW propagation control through engineered arrays.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework for topological stability using patterned anisotropy. It then uses simulations to compare DMI-free vs. DMI-present states, culminating in a demonstration of how these structures can function as reconfigurable magnonic elements controlling spin waves.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of engineering local symmetries and topological defects (skyrmions) for controlled wave propagation shares conceptual links with engineered quantum waveguides or artificial lattices used in AMO physics.
